intro: Use comparative adverbs to compare how two actions happen and superlative adverbs for the highest or lowest degree of an action in a group. Keep the adverb rule separate from the adjective rule.

sections.title: Short adverbs: -er and -est
sections.text: Fast, hard, high, low and long take -er and -est: faster/fastest and harder/hardest. For spelling, late → later → latest: add -r and -st. Early → earlier → earliest: change y to i before -er/-est.
examples: The library opened earliest on Thursday.

sections.title: Most -ly adverbs: more and most
sections.text: Most adverbs ending in -ly use more and most: more carefully, most carefully; more easily, most easily. Do not add -er/-est, double letters, or change -ly to -lier/-liest.
examples: Asha explained the instructions more clearly than before.
sections.note: Early is a conventional exception: earlier/earliest is the usual form in these comparison exercises.

sections.title: Irregular forms and far
sections.text: Well → better → best. Badly usually becomes worse/worst; more badly and most badly can also be natural when the manner or extent of harm is the focus. Both farther/farthest and further/furthest are standard for distance; further alone also means additional or broader.
examples: The team explained the plan better than before.
The rain damaged the paper sign most badly.

sections.title: Common mistakes to avoid
sections.text: Use faster, not more fast. Use more easily, not easilier. Do not combine two comparison patterns, and do not copy the adjective rule onto an -ly adverb.
examples: The team finished faster than before.
The new instructions can be followed more easily.

sections.title: Than, optional the, and hardly
sections.text: Use than after a comparative: more quickly than the other team. With superlative adverbs, the is often used but can be omitted when both sound natural: She ran the fastest / She ran fastest. Hard means with effort; hardly means almost not, so it is not the comparative of hard.
examples: Of the runners, Eva ran the fastest.
I could hardly hear the announcement.

miniCheck.sentence: Our group spoke _____ than last time.
miniCheck.explanation: Clearly is an -ly adverb, so use more clearly than.

miniCheck.sentence: Of the three teams, Aisha performed _____.
miniCheck.explanation: Well is irregular as an adverb: well → better → best. The is also natural: performed the best.

miniCheck.sentence: Of the three buses, route 2 arrived _____.
miniCheck.explanation: Early is the -ly exception: early → earlier → earliest. The earliest is also natural in this adverbial position.
